title: Cadena RTS [RTS Other Hybrid] – an RTS where every bullet has to be physically carried from the mine to the front. Free in-browser prototype, looking for  ▎ feedback.
author: apenara12
selftext:
Hi all,

I'm building Cadena RTS, a 1v1 RTS against an AI faction where the interesting part isn't the fight, it's the supply line behind it. It's free, runs in the browser, no install and no account.

  [https://lgavice.itch.io/cadena-rts](https://lgavice.itch.io/cadena-rts)

The premise

Every bullet a unit fires came out of a mine you own, went through a factory you own and arrived on a truck you own. There are no resource counters that fill themselves — everything is physically hauled across the map by people, on foot or by truck. Cut someone's chain and their front goes quiet.

  


  Four rules the whole thing is built on:



  \- Soldiers are equipped, not trained. Every unit starts as the same recruit and becomes a rifleman, an AT team, an engineer or a tank crew by picking up a kit. Your economy and your army are the same pool of people, so arming someone is always a decision about who stops working.

  \- Nodes are built on, not captured. You don't click a mine to own it. You build an extractor on top of it, and someone has to walk over there to do it.

  \- Nothing gets built without recruits. Every building is a work site that recruits have to carry steel to. There is no instant purchase anywhere in the game.       

  \- Nothing is yours until it reaches your base. Ore sitting in a silo is not money.



  What that produces in play



  \- Three chains competing for the same hands: mine → foundry → steel, oil field → well → refinery → fuel, steel → alloy works → alloy. You never have enough people for all three at once.

  \- Fuel does three jobs simultaneously: it lights your base, it moves your vehicles and it makes heavy ammunition. With no fuel a vehicle doesn't die — it becomes a turret. It stays where it is and keeps firing.

  \- Fog of war with three states: explored, visible, and heard. A listening post gives no vision at all. It leaves blurred marks where something moved, and won't tell you what it was or whose it was.

  \- A map generated fresh every match, symmetric by 180° rotation, with mountain ranges you can only cross through two or three passes. You can build roads, dig tunnels under the rock, and mine the roads.



  Where it honestly is



  It's a grey prototype. There is no art — everything is drawn with primitives on purpose, so it looks closer to a diagram than to a game. Single player against one  

  AI. Full Spanish and English, guided tutorial, F1 for controls. The build up there is from last week; I'm mid-rework on the energy system right now, so a few things will move.

  
\*\*Built with AI assistance on the code; the design and the numbers are mine.\*\*



  What I'd actually like feedback on



  1. Does hauling everything by hand feel like a real decision, or just busywork?

  2. Is the AI a credible opponent, or does it fall over once you know what you're doing?

  3. Is it legible? It's a lot of systems with no art to carry them.



  Happy to answer anything.

comments.author: _Saturn1
comments.body: (Commenting so i remember to try it)

comments.author: Kitchen-Many-8466
comments.body: how does the ai handle the "i need to send a carrier to the mine but also i'm about to lose the front" tradeoff? like does it even model that as a decision or does it just run a fixed ratio of supply units vs combat units?

replies.author: apenara12
replies.body:
Neither, really. Hauling and fighting are separate pools: carriers are unarmed recruits and trucks, soldiers are recruits who've been handed a kit, so a squad never gets pulled off the line to carry ore. Where they compete is the production queue, and there economy wins by design. 

Each tick the AI works out how many carriers its mines actually need (production rate × trip distance ÷ load × speed) and trains recruits until that's covered. Only then does it equip squads, capped by how many nodes it holds and whether it can pay upkeep. 

Emergencies are handled inside each pool: a dry oil well steals a carrier from a steel mine, and a clogged refinery steals one from a node. What it doesn't have is a "we're losing the front" signal. It guards its least-defended outpost and attacks on a timer, but under pressure it doesn't shift production toward soldiers. 

Honestly, losing a node lowers its soldier cap, which is backwards.

comments.author: Maple-Syrup89
comments.body:
I tried it, I have played lots of old school command and conquer, but this was a bit hard to understand. I did the tutorial but some of the steps flew by so quickly I couldn't read them. It seemed to get stuck on step 8. 

I couldn't figure out how to resupply. The tutorial AI didn't fight back, perhaps obviously. I would have been stomped though for the lack of understanding above. Controls felt almost familiar but guys would just start doing something on their own when I clicked something I thought was totally different. 

I feel like the premise and style of game us up my alley but controls were hard to master. Also camera not following mouse was a bit tough as well, would have wanted a mix of WASD and let the mouse move the camera was well.
